fatal_errors: The proposed humid oxidative annealing intervention does not reconstruct the target intervention, which was a closed-loop high-throughput synthesis, post-ageing screening, machine-learning, Bayesian-optimisation, and inverse-analysis campaign.

The cited evidence does not establish that annealing an existing near-equiatomic alloy will generate the claimed nanoporous high-entropy oxide layer; the supporting studies concern separately synthesized high-entropy oxides or Pt deposited on such oxides.
Neither citation supports the predicted below-150 °C light-off, resistance to NO poisoning, or simultaneous treatment of CO, hydrocarbons, and NO under a near-stoichiometric multicomponent exhaust.
The asserted deficiencies of the unmodified catalyst are not measured or evidenced, and the relevant Pd/Al2O3 and random-exploration baselines are omitted.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested activity–poisoning–durability problem and proposes a testable treated-versus-untreated comparison. High-entropy oxides can plausibly improve thermal stability and CO oxidation, so this is a scientifically plausible alternative rather than an entirely unsupported idea. However, it diverges fundamentally from the hidden target's discovery intervention, Cu–Pt electronic reconstruction mechanism, synthesis-variable dependence, and post-ageing Pd benchmark. Its conditions are generic and differ from the specified 900 °C lean/rich hydrothermal ageing and multicomponent 100–500 °C test feed. The evidence supports entropy-related stability only indirectly and does not validate formation of the proposed layer by post-treatment, NO/H2O poisoning resistance, hydrocarbon conversion, or sub-150 °C performance. The falsification experiment is directionally useful but needs a fixed full exhaust composition, ageing protocol, statistical replication, and structural measurements confirming whether the proposed oxide mediator actually forms.
